fields.Front: What are the two possible sources of energy behind natural disasters and catastrophes?
fields.Back: Energy internal to Earth (drives earthquakes, tsunami, volcanic eruptions) and energy external to Earth (drives hurricanes, climate change, asteroid impacts).

fields.Front: List the steps of the scientific method in order (as in the Unit 1 reading).
fields.Back: Observation(s) -> hypothesis -> experiment/test -> (publication) -> further testing -> theory -> prediction -> after very long, always-successful testing, a law.

fields.Text: In the scientific method, a {{c1::hypothesis}} is formed from observations; successful hypotheses build a {{c2::theory}}, which after very long successful testing is reworded as a {{c3::law}}.

fields.Front: In the scientific method, does a successful theory prove its predictions absolutely?
fields.Back: No. Testing never stops; a single contrary observation (one rude poodle) overturns the theory and you start over.

fields.Text: {{c1::Bertrand Russell}} (1928, The Outline of Philosophy) wrote that scientists are 'slow to believe, and never speak without modification'.
fields.Extra: Bertrand Russell, 1928, The Outline of Philosophy.

fields.Front: Define 'natural process' (course definition).
fields.Back: An event directed by physical, chemical and biological activity, e.g. earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, hurricanes.

fields.Front: When does a natural process become a 'natural hazard'?
fields.Back: When it is a potential threat to life or property (property ranging from a person's home to a shoreline prone to erosion).

fields.Front: According to the reading, why do disasters commonly occur?
fields.Back: Because of careless appraisal of a natural hazard.

fields.Front: What is 'assessing risk' in the Unit 1 reading?
fields.Back: Learning the conditions that precede hazardous processes (precursor signs / process indicators) so we can predict them, reduce their effects, and get out of the way.

fields.Front: Dictionary definition of 'disaster' used in the course?
fields.Back: A sudden or great misfortune; a calamity.

fields.Front: What is the key difference between a disaster and a catastrophe?
fields.Back: Scale: disasters are local scale; catastrophes are regional to global scale and totally disrupt or end a society.

fields.Front: Name the four levels of the instructor's qualitative disaster/catastrophe scale.
fields.Back: Local disaster, regional disaster, regional catastrophe, global catastrophe.

fields.Front: Define 'local disaster' (course scale).
fields.Back: A significant disruption to local society and communities, but the consequences are contained locally.

fields.Front: Define 'regional disaster' (course scale).
fields.Back: Disruption greater than a single city area might occupy, with more widespread consequences.

fields.Front: Define 'regional catastrophe' (course scale).
fields.Back: Disruption of sufficient magnitude that large regions (provinces, states, countries) must deal with the consequences, including death and numerous injuries to the regional population.

fields.Front: Define 'global catastrophe' (course scale).
fields.Back: Disruption felt and dealt with on a global scale; death of many whole species is common.

fields.Text: On the course scale, the 1985 Mexico City earthquake was a {{c1::regional disaster}}; the 1976 Tangshan earthquake was a {{c2::regional catastrophe}}.
On the course scale, the 2004 Boxing Day earthquake-tsunami was a {{c1::global catastrophe (low end)}}; the 65.5 Ma asteroid impact was a {{c2::global catastrophe (high end)}}.

fields.Front: What happened to the Hotel de Carlo in Mexico City in 1985?
fields.Back: Two closely spaced buildings swayed and banged repeatedly against each other until one middle section collapsed, killing occupants; damage was widespread across the city and region.

fields.Text: The {{c1::1976}} Tangshan (China) earthquake officially killed {{c2::250,000}} (residents say 400,000-600,000) of ~1 million - a {{c3::regional catastrophe}} and the first modern giant quake centred beneath a large city.
fields.Extra: Official 250,000; residents say over 400,000 and possibly 600,000; urban region of nearly 1 million, so at least one third killed. First modern instance of a very large quake centred directly beneath a large city.

fields.Text: The {{c1::26 December 2004}} Indian Ocean earthquake was the {{c2::second}} largest ever recorded; its tsunami killed at least {{c3::230,000}} and was detected on tide gauges in Vancouver.
fields.Extra: Second largest earthquake ever recorded; tsunami killed at least 230,000 (mostly drowning); felt worldwide, triggered quakes as far as Alaska, detected on tide gauges in Vancouver.

fields.Front: What happened about 65.5 million years ago and what fraction of species died?
fields.Back: A very large asteroid made an enormous crater in Mexico; approximately 70% of all species went extinct (Chapter 1 says 65-70%).

fields.Front: Why does the course exclude famine, and what famine statistics does it cite?
fields.Back: Famine is largely man-made. 1900-1969: 110.5 million famine deaths worldwide, 59.5 million in China alone (1958-1969).

fields.Text: In the 1950s the average cost of hazardous processes was a 'mere' {{c1::$3.9 billion}} per year.
fields.Extra: A 'mere' $3.9 billion per year (EM-DAT data; costs have risen dramatically since).

fields.Front: Does the rising cost of disasters mean there are more severe eruptions and earthquakes now?
fields.Back: No. Population has greatly increased and people live closer to known hazards (volcano slopes, fault zones) with more expensive infrastructure.

fields.Text: World population was about {{c1::300 million}} in 0 AD and {{c2::7.3 billion}} today; at the current rate it would reach {{c3::384 billion}} by 2300.

fields.Front: Complete: 'If disasters are having a greater impact today, it's primarily the result of ...'
fields.Back: '... human nature rather than Mother Nature.' More people can be affected, and expensive infrastructure is built in hazard-prone areas (coasts, fire-prone forests, steep slopes, flood plains).

fields.Front: Why do people put themselves in harm's way (reading)?
fields.Back: A combination of arrogance and ignorance plus sheer numbers; over-reliance on early warning technology; and benefits of hazardous areas (fertile volcanic soils, fertile Nile banks, coastal fisheries and transport).

fields.Text: Big disasters of the decade: 2004 Indonesian tsunami (~{{c1::230,000}} dead), 2008 Myanmar {{c2::Nargis}} Cyclone (~150,000), 2010 {{c3::Haiti}} earthquake (Red Cross 50,000; government 300,000).
fields.Extra: 2004 Indonesian earthquake-tsunami (~230,000); 2008 Myanmar Nargis Cyclone (~150,000); 2010 Haiti earthquake (Red Cross 50,000; Haitian government 300,000).

fields.Text: 'The Mother of all Extinctions', about {{c1::251}} million years ago, wiped out about {{c2::96%}} of all species on Earth.
fields.Extra: An extinction event about 251 million years ago that wiped out about 96% of all species on Earth.

fields.Text: The reading claims that in the last {{c1::150}} years humans caused more damage to Earth than in the previous {{c2::7 thousand}} years, and that population might stabilize at {{c3::12 billion}} within 100 years.
